title: Defending it when people ask in earnest
promise: You'll prepare your project's defence: justifying why you chose what you chose, answering what you don't know without going blank, and holding up under the hard questions. By the end you'll have been through a full dry run.
why: Nuria defended her system to a partner at a large practice. It was going well until he asked: «why Claude and not ChatGPT?». She went blank. The truth was she had started with Claude because a friend used it, and it had worked for her. That was a perfectly valid answer and she didn't give it; she said something muddled about model quality that didn't hold up. She lost more credibility with that sentence than she would have with any technical fault in the system.

theory.title: Defending isn't proving you're clever
theory.text: When someone asks in earnest about your project they aren't trying to catch you out: they're trying to work out whether they can rely on you. And what people rely on isn't that you know everything, it's that you know where the edges of what you know are. That's why a defence isn't about having an answer for everything, it's about every answer being honest and backed. An answer starting «I don't know, but I can find out like this» adds to you. One that invents a technical justification subtracts, and subtracts far more than people think, because whoever is asking usually knows their own ground better than you do.
theory.analogy: It's the same as with the AI's answers: a cited source is worth more than a confident sentence. And a well-worded invention is the worst of the lot.
theory.example: «I started with Claude because it was recommended to me, I tested both with my documents and Claude got 27 out of 30 while the other got 24» is a complete answer. And it's the truth.

theory.title: Every decision is justified by what you ruled out
theory.text: «Why this and not that?» is the question that comes up most and the one people carry least prepared. A good answer has three parts: which options you looked at, what criterion you chose on, and what would have made you choose differently. That third part is what convinces, because it shows the decision was a decision and not an accident. And it works even when the original reason was daft: «I started here because it was what I had to hand, then I compared it with this other on this criterion, and I stayed with this one» is a perfect answer. What doesn't work is inventing a technical reason after the fact.
theory.example: «I looked at Claude and ChatGPT. The criterion was which got more right with my documents, which I measured with 30 questions. If I'd needed my team to use it from several accounts, I'd have gone to the other one on price.»

theory.title: What you don't know gets answered in three parts
theory.text: You'll be asked things you don't know, and that isn't a failure: it's normal. What decides is how you say it. The formula that works has three parts and can be learned: you say you don't know, you say how you'd find out, and you give the timescale. «I haven't measured it. I can measure it by running the question set with that configuration, and I'll have it tomorrow.» With that, the conversation moves on and you come across as someone who knows how to work. What sinks people isn't not knowing, it's the hesitation, the «well, it depends» and making something up rather than admitting it.
theory.example: Nuria should have said: «I haven't compared the two on a year's cost. I can do it from this month's usage and you'll have it Thursday.» Ten seconds and the subject closes well.

theory.title: The trap questions and how to take each one
theory.text: There are four that recur. «Doesn't anyone do this already?»: answered with what your setup has that a generic one doesn't, which is usually your documents, your criteria and your checks. «And what if it gets it wrong?»: with block 08, warnings, undo and the approval point. «What happens when you're not around?»: with the handover from lesson 45, which exists precisely for that. And «isn't this risky with the data?»: with block 09, the three piles and what you checked about the provider. Notice that all four are answered with work you've already done. The defence isn't prepared at the end: it's prepared by doing the earlier blocks properly.
theory.example: «And what if it gets it wrong?» → «It gets 27 out of 30 right and I know which kind of question it fails on, it's written down. Anything going outwards passes my approval, and if it fails a warning reaches me the same day.»

theory.title: Admitting a weakness in front of everyone adds to you
theory.text: If something about your project is weak, say so before they find it. It completely changes how it lands: said by you it's a conscious decision with a plan; found by them it's an oversight. And they almost always will find it, because someone asking in earnest has experience. The form is short: what's weak, why you left it that way, and what you'd do with more time. Three sentences and you move on. What you don't do is apologise at length or say sorry for the whole project.
theory.example: «It doesn't query the scanned documents, that's 14 out of 192 and I decided not to invest in converting them because they're barely consulted. If this grew, it'd be the first thing I'd do.»

theory.title: Bring the paperwork, not your memory
theory.text: In a defence you don't have to remember anything: you have to know where each thing is. Bring open or to hand the files you've built along the way: the exam with its results, the checks, the breakdown log, the cost sum, the data and tools document. When they ask you for a figure, you show it rather than recalling it. That does two things: it takes the memory pressure off you and it demonstrates the work exists. It is, by some distance, what impresses most in a defence, and it requires knowing nothing extra.
theory.example: «How often does it get it right?» → opens the file and shows it. «Here's the exam: 27 out of 30, and here's the breakdown by kind of question.» End of discussion.

tasks.title: List your decisions
tasks.action: Write the five or six important decisions you took in your project: which tool, which model, what gets automated and what doesn't, which data goes in, where it's hosted. For each one write the three parts: which options you looked at, what criterion you chose on, and what would have made you choose otherwise.
tasks.expect: Five or six decisions with their three parts. If for one of them you don't recall looking at alternatives, write exactly that: «I started here because it was what I had» is a valid and honest answer.
tasks.stuck: If the third part is hard, turn it around: in what situation would your decision have been the wrong one? That's precisely what would have made you choose otherwise.

tasks.title: Prepare the four usual answers
tasks.action: Write the answer to the four trap questions, each in two sentences and with a fact from your files: and anyone could do this, and what if it gets it wrong, what happens when you're not around, and isn't this risky with the data. Next to each answer note which of your files holds the fact backing it.
tasks.expect: Four short answers with their file beside them. If one has no file behind it, you have outstanding work from the earlier blocks.
tasks.stuck: If you don't have the answer to «what happens when you're not around?», the handover from lesson 45 is missing. It's the question that most exposes a project living only inside someone's head.

tasks.title: Write your three weak points
tasks.action: Be honest with yourself: which three things about your project are weak. For each, three sentences: what's weak, why you left it that way, and what you'd do with more time or more budget. You're going to say them yourself, before they're found.
tasks.expect: Three points with their justification. Read them aloud: if they sound like an apology, rewrite them as a decision. «I decided not to do it because…» rather than «I didn't have time to…».
tasks.stuck: If you think you have no weak points, you have a very big one: you haven't looked. Ask someone to use your setup for half an hour and tell you what grated.

tasks.title: Prepare the folder you take to the defence
tasks.action: Gather in one folder, or in open tabs, everything you might need to show: the exam with results, the checks, the breakdown log, the cost sum, the data and tools file, the handover package. Give them names you can find in two seconds with someone watching you.
tasks.expect: A folder or a set of tabs. Rehearse opening three of them quickly: if any takes you more than five seconds to find, rename it.
tasks.stuck: If files are missing because you skipped blocks, that's the signal for what to complete before defending. Start with the exam from lesson 34 and the checks from lesson 35: those are the two most often asked for.

tasks.title: Run a dry run with the AI as the panel
tasks.action: Set up a real interrogation. Give it the context and ask it to question you one at a time, without showing all the questions up front, so it resembles the real thing.
tasks.prompt:
You're going to act as the panel for my project defence. You aren't friendly: you're someone experienced who wants to know whether this holds up.

MY PROJECT: [describe what it does, who for and with which tools]
MY DECISIONS: [paste your list with the three parts]
MY WEAK POINTS: [paste the three]

RULES FOR THE DRY RUN:
1. Ask me ONE question at a time and wait for my answer. Don't give me the whole list.
2. If my answer is vague, leans on something I haven't measured, or sounds like an excuse, say so and press on that same point. Don't move to another topic.
3. After eight questions, stop and tell me: which I answered worst, which answer sounded invented, and what I'm missing having prepared.

Start with the first question.
tasks.expect: Eight questions and a closing diagnosis. It's normal to discover two or three answers you thought were fine that don't hold up when someone presses.
tasks.stuck: If it asks questions too technical for your project, say: «Ask as [a client / my manager / a teacher] would, not as an engineer.» The character changes the kind of question a great deal.

tasks.title: Rehearse it with a person and record yourself
tasks.where: With someone in front of you
tasks.action: Tell them the project in five minutes as in the previous lesson and ask them to question you for five minutes afterwards, with permission to press if an answer doesn't convince them. Record the audio. Listening back, look for two things: where you hesitate and where you say something you can't back with a file.
tasks.expect: A recording and two or three things to improve. The hesitation is almost always in the same place: the question you knew was coming and hadn't fully prepared.
tasks.stuck: If recording yourself embarrasses you, do it anyway and delete it afterwards. Hearing yourself is uncomfortable and it's what improves a defence fastest: you hear yourself say «well, in principle…» and you never say it again.

matters: That defending isn't knowing everything, it's knowing your edges and being able to show the work.
That a decision is justified by saying what you ruled out and what would have made you choose otherwise.
That what you don't know gets answered in three parts: I don't know, this is how I'd find out, by when.
That the four trap questions are answered with the work from the earlier blocks.
ignore: Learning answers by heart. You bring the folder and you show it.
Justifying decisions with technical reasons that weren't yours.
Getting defensive about criticism. You acknowledge it and move on.
canDo: Justify every decision with options, criterion and alternative.
Answer what you don't know without losing credibility.
Get ahead of your weak points so they count in your favour.
Show the figure rather than recall it.
cantDo: Defend a project where you've measured nothing.
Improvise answers to the four usual questions.
Stop them asking about what's weak.
Substitute confident delivery for work not done.
words: Which options you looked at, what criterion you chose on and what would have made you choose otherwise.
I don't know + how I'd find out + by when. The way to answer what you don't know.
What you know is weak and say yourself before it's found.
The files to hand so you can show the figure rather than recall it.
Rehearsing the interrogation beforehand, with someone who presses when an answer is vague.
next: You can tell it and defend it. Lesson 48 is about what almost nobody on the course considers and where the money actually is: turning this into something that can be sold more than once.
